<header class="tour-header">

<h1>Inside Bali's Incredible Regenerative Farmstead: Growing Food With Nature</h1>

<div class="tour-categories">
  <span class="tour-category">Indonesia</span>
  <span class="tour-category">Bali</span>
  <span class="tour-category">Food Forest Tours</span>
  <span class="tour-category">Regenerative Agriculture</span>
  <span class="tour-category">Tropical Gardening</span>
  <span class="tour-category">Seed Saving</span>
</div>

<p class="tour-description">
Explore Bali Regenerative Farmstead with Hayley and local farmer Made, from grafted eggplants and seed saving to biodiversity, tropical crops and regenerative education.
</p>

<div class="tour-meta">
  <div>
    <span class="meta-label">Host</span>
    <span class="meta-value">Hayley, Thriving with Nature</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span class="meta-label">Episode</span>
    <span class="meta-value">Part 1</span>
  </div>
</div>

</header>

<p class="tour-lead">
In the mountains of central Bali, just a kilometer from a protected ancient
rainforest, Hayley and local farmer Made are transforming former monocropped
land into a diverse regenerative garden. Vegetables, herbs, flowers and tropical
crops share space with bees, butterflies and beneficial insects. Joined by my
son Sebastian, I explore a garden where experimentation, observation and a
connection with nature are as important as the food being harvested.
</p>

<section class="quick-facts" aria-label="Tour snapshot">

<section class="tour-section">

<h2>Inside Bali Regenerative Farmstead</h2>

<p>
Hayley describes the farmstead as a passion project that began five or six
years before our visit. Having lived in Bali for 13 years, she wanted to build
a life that allowed her to thrive with nature. The property sits about 700
meters above sea level, where she estimates temperatures are around six
degrees Celsius cooler than lower areas of the island.
</p>

<p>
The nearby rainforest provides inspiration for the landscape she hopes to
create. Rather than operating solely as a conventional production farm, Hayley
sees the property as a place to demonstrate how a diverse ecosystem can
produce food throughout the year.
</p>

<p>
Our first tour focuses on the vegetable and herb garden, where familiar crops
grow alongside tropical alternatives. The garden is still evolving, and the
successes and challenges Hayley shares make it particularly interesting to
explore.
</p>

</section>

<section class="tour-section">

<h2>What You’ll Learn From Bali Regenerative Farmstead</h2>

<div class="learn-grid">

  <div class="learn-item">
    How Hayley and Made are rebuilding diversity on formerly monocropped land
  </div>

  <div class="learn-item">
    How grafting eggplants onto locally adapted rootstock improved production in this garden
  </div>

  <div class="learn-item">
    Why observing insects can help reveal relationships between pests and predators
  </div>

  <div class="learn-item">
    How seed saving and tropical alternatives help adapt the garden to local conditions
  </div>

  <div class="learn-item">
    How vetiver grass serves several purposes in the landscape
  </div>

  <div class="learn-item">
    What Hayley hopes to achieve through self-sufficiency and regenerative education
  </div>

</div>

</section>

<section class="tour-section">

<h2>Three Highlights From Bali Regenerative Farmstead</h2>

<div class="short-grid">

  <article class="short-card">

    <div class="short-video">

      <iframe
        src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/S0KTT_pdmtw?rel=0"
        title="Bali Regenerative Farmstead — Highlight 1"
        loading="lazy"
        allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share"
        referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
        allowfullscreen>
      </iframe>

    </div>

    <div class="short-copy">

      <h3>Bali Regenerative Farmstead — Highlight 1</h3>

<section class="tour-section">

<h2>Transforming Monocropped Land Into a Thriving Ecosystem</h2>

<p>
One of the most memorable stories from the tour begins with hundreds of
caterpillars. When Hayley and Made first planted salad greens on land
previously managed with chemicals, the young plants attracted an overwhelming
number of caterpillars. Made was understandably concerned, but Hayley wanted
to observe what would happen before intervening.
</p>

<p>
Several weeks later, Made sent Hayley a video of a wasp feeding on a
caterpillar. Ants also began taking caterpillars, and Hayley says the garden
has not experienced the same problem since. This is an account of what
happened on their property, rather than a guarantee that every pest problem
will resolve without intervention.
</p>

<p>
Flowers such as zinnias and marigolds are woven through the vegetable beds.
Some crops are allowed to flower and set seed, providing resources for insects
as well as future plantings. Hayley watches for ladybirds and praying mantises
as signs of predator activity.
</p>

<p>
Made is central to the story. Hayley credits his openness to new methods,
enthusiasm for regenerative agriculture and ongoing work with much of the
garden’s progress. Their partnership illustrates how experimentation and local
knowledge can develop together.
</p>

</section>

<section class="tour-section">

<h2>Adapting to Bali’s Tropical Growing Conditions</h2>

<p>
Growing familiar vegetables in a tropical climate has required Hayley to
rethink some of her favorite crops. Strawberries struggle with heavy rain,
while tomatoes have been more successful during the extended dry season.
During our visit, we taste both red and golden cherry tomatoes, and Hayley
discusses her hope of eventually growing tomatoes under cover during the wet
season.
</p>

<p>
Eggplants offer one of the most striking examples of adaptation. Earlier
attempts produced only a few fruits before they rotted or fell. Grafting
cultivated purple eggplants onto a locally adapted, spiny eggplant rootstock
has given Hayley a much more continuous supply. Made is preparing another
graft during the tour.
</p>

<p>
Red and green amaranth, known locally as bayam, have become alternatives to
the spinach Hayley grew up eating. Sweet potatoes have similarly become a more
successful crop for her than ordinary potatoes. These choices show how a
garden can evolve around the plants that perform well in its own climate.
</p>

<p>
The herb garden adds another dimension. Hayley combines chocolate mint with
stevia for a sweet tasting experience and tarragon with stevia for a licorice-
like flavor. Lemon balm, dill, garlic chives and mitsuba provide additional
variety. She also saves seeds from her salad crops and says she has not
purchased seeds in a couple of years.
</p>

</section>

<section class="tour-section">

<h2>Growing Toward Self-Sufficiency and Regenerative Education</h2>

<p>
Hayley hopes to reach around 80 percent self-sufficiency at the farmstead. Her
first soybean experiment is particularly personal: she would love to produce
the soybeans needed for her own tempeh. Pineapples, cassava and several kinds
of sweet potato already add diversity to the garden.
</p>

<p>
Vetiver grass illustrates her interest in plants that perform multiple
functions. At the farmstead it helps stabilize the garden edges, supplies cut
material for mulch and is planted near the greywater system. Torch ginger also
connects the garden to local culinary traditions through its use in sambal.
</p>

<p>
Looking ahead, Hayley envisions a syntropic agroforestry demonstration
inspired by the nearby rainforest, an educational center, a farm café and
potentially a soil laboratory. She imagines local farmers bringing soil
samples to observe microbial life under a microscope. These are future
ambitions rather than completed facilities.
</p>

<p>
Her childhood experiences in the rainforest on Australia’s Christmas Island
and her interest in the Ringing Cedars book series have helped shape her
personal connection with nature. The tour offers a glimpse of how those
influences inform the farmstead’s evolving philosophy.
</p>

</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>The Green Yard Takeaway</h2>
<div class="takeaway">
<p>
What stands out about Hayley and Made’s garden is not just the diversity of
food growing there, but the willingness to observe and adapt. From grafting
eggplants to saving seeds and watching insects establish relationships, the
farmstead is a living experiment shaped by its surroundings.
</p>
<p>
Abundance can mean more than a harvest. It can also mean a landscape filled
with life, a partnership that builds knowledge, and a place where others can
learn. Bali Regenerative Farmstead offers an inspiring example of that vision
as it continues to develop.
</p>
</div>
</section>
